title: Successive governments asleep at the wheel on social care, says head of review
description: And she said the failings identified by the recent Covid inquiry report into social care were testament to that.Last month the inquiry published a rep
body: And she said the failings identified by the recent Covid inquiry report into social care were testament to that.Last month the inquiry published a report which said the care sector appeared to be "something of an afterthought" in the early stages of the pandemic, allowing Covid to spread like "wildfire".Baroness Casey, who will address a conference of social care leaders later on Wednesday, said the findings were "so awful" and "a national shame"."Successive governments have been asleep at the wheel. We've got our heads in the sand."Her final recommendations for services for older people and adults with disabilities, including care homes, will be published next summer.It comes as her commission publishes research showing England is an international outlier for having no "clear system of stewardship" for social care, unlike countries such as France and Germany.She said the market was dominated by private providers and said the regulator – the Care Quality Commission – as being a "spectator at the site of a car crash".The research found:Two people with the same condition having different experiences depending on where they live – different assement processes, waits and levels of supportThose who paid for their own care – social care is means-tested – are charged on average 40% more than the councils pay for care they arrangeWhen Andy Burnham became prime minister, he said social care was one of his key priorities although the Casey commission was set up by the Starmer government."Together, we can build a new settlement for care," Baroness Casey said."One based on values I still believe this country shares – decency, contribution and a duty to care for our neighbours, our loved ones and ourselves."

schema.headline: Successive governments asleep at the wheel on social care, says head of review

title: New photos 'essential evidence' of possible SAS war crimes, inquiry hears
description: An inquiry into UK special forces operations in Afghanistan has released photos described as "essential evidence", showing soldiers could have execute
body: An inquiry into UK special forces operations in Afghanistan has released photos described as "essential evidence", showing soldiers could have executed unarmed people lying asleep.For the first time, the inquiry has made public photos taken of the deceased, across two SAS operations, that show multiple individuals lying in bed with shots to the head.The inquiry's lead barrister, Oliver Glasgow KC, said the photos may be evidence of possible war crimes and worthy of expert interrogation.The public inquiry is examining allegations that the SAS murdered unarmed civilians and detainees on night raids between 2010 and 2013 and planted weapons to cover up the killings.The graphic photographs show multiple unarmed people lying in bed. One person was tucked under a floral blanket, others with their heads on pillows, blood pooling around their heads. Blood spatter is visible low on the wall in one of the images, consistent with someone being shot while lying down.Glasgow described how many "look like they sustained head shots" and in a number of cases "there appears to be a dead body with his head on a pillow".He said further analysis may be able to confirm if the people in the photographs were "shot when asleep".Seventeen people were killed across the two operations which took place in Helmand province in 2011. The youngest of those killed in each of the operations were 15 and 14 years old respectively.Glasgow said the photos appeared to contradict the accounts given by the SAS and would have raised serious questions for the military police officers investigating the operations as potential murders.Lt Col John Harvey, who led the military police's murder probe, agreed they "didn't look right". He told the inquiry his team were clear the photos could be vital evidence.Despite the repeated requests of the police investigators to submit the photographs for further testing, this never took place.One of the investigators, speaking on the condition of anonymity, told the BBC "you can see why we were concerned", adding: "Bullet marks on the walls so low to the ground appeared to undermine the special forces' version of events."The inquiry is subjecting the photographs to expert forensic analysis.BBC Panorama has been investigating allegations the SAS executed unarmed civilians and children for more than eight years. The public inquiry was established in 2022 in the wake of Panorama's revelations.The photos appear to support the findings of Panorama's 2022 investigation into raids in Helmand province which took place a decade before.Panorama travelled to Afghanistan to gather evidence related to four raids on homes that killed 26 people.The BBC visited the same guesthouses where the photographs released by the inquiry on Tuesday were taken. Panorama's team were the first British investigators to visit the sites of the shootings, despite a five-year-long military police investigation.Official special forces accounts of the incidents claim Taliban insurgents opened fire on troops as they entered the compounds, forcing the SAS to return fire and kill those inside.However weaponry experts told the BBC evidence collected by Panorama indicated multiple rounds appeared to have been fired from above.This suggests those killed were either lying down or sitting against the wall and not in a firefight.Family members also told Panorama those killed had been shot cleanly in the head or chest - a common characteristic of a deliberate SAS shooting at close range.The photographs released by the inquiry show multiple "traumatic injuries to the head or face" of those killed by the SAS, according to its lead barrister.The inquiry also heard evidence that calls into question whether alleged war crimes were thoroughly investigated.  It heard how investigators were still in Afghanistan in July 2019 gathering evidence as senior officers prepared to close their murder investigation and inform ministers. The military police investigators were looking for eyewitnesses to unlawful killings and the planting of weapons.One member of the Afghan partner unit that served on operations alongside the SAS told military police he had personally witnessed a British soldier planting a rifle on an unarmed person after they had been killed.Do you have information about this story that you want to share?Get in touch using SecureDrop, a highly anonymous and secure way of whistleblowing to the BBC which uses the TOR network.Or by using the Signal messaging app, an end-to-end encrypted message service designed to protect your data.SecureDrop: http://kt2bqe753wj6dgarak2ryj4d6a5tccrivbvod5ab3uxhug5fi624vsqd.onion/Signal: 0044 7714 956 936Please note that the SecureDrop link will only work in a Tor browser. For information on keeping secure and anonymous, here's some advice on how to use SecureDrop.

title: I'm A Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here! 2026 - see the line-up in full
description: Wayne Rooney leads I'm A Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here! line-upImage source, ITVImage caption, Eleven celebrities will enter the Australian jungle c
body: Wayne Rooney leads I'm A Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here! line-upImage source, ITVImage caption, Eleven celebrities will enter the Australian jungle camp on MondayByEmma Saunders and Ian YoungsCulture reportersFormer England and Manchester United footballer Wayne Rooney, Gavin and Stacey star Joanna Page and YouTuber Sharky will be among the intrepid crew entering the jungle Down Under for this year's I'm A Celebrity... Get Me Out Of Here!They will be joined by Kaiser Chiefs frontman Ricky Wilson, Paralympian and presenter Ade Adepitan, actress Claire Sweeney and broadcaster Mariella Frostrup.TV presenter AJ  Odudu, comedian Jack Skipper, Love Island contestant Chloe Burrows and model Leomie Anderson round out the team headed for Australia.Hosts Ant and Dec will return with the ITV show's opening episode on Monday, 16 November, with the series now in its 26th year.Image source, ITVImage caption, Wayne Rooney said he wants to go one better than wife Coleen, who was runner-up in 2024Ade Adepitan - Paralympian and documentary maker, who will be the first wheelchair user in the show's historyLeomie Anderson - Model and co-host of Glow Up: Britain's Next Make-Up Star Chloe Burrows - Love Island finalist, Kiss Radio breakfast presenter and host of Chloe vs The World podcastMariella Frostrup - Broadcaster, author and journalist, including appearances on Loose Women and Times RadioAJ Odudu - Big Brother presenter and former Strictly Come Dancing contestantJoanna Page - Stacey from hit sitcom Gavin and Stacey, and host of TV series including Shift the Thrift and Shop Well For LessWayne Rooney - Former Everton, Manchester United and England striker  turned football manager and punditSharky - one of YouTube's Beta Squad (alongside Celebrity Traitors star King Kenny among others), who have 12 million subscribersJack Skipper - Stand-up comedian and social media starClaire Sweeney - Coronation Street and Brookside star and musical actressRicky Wilson - Kaiser Chiefs singer, ex-Virgin Radio drivetime host and former The Voice UK coachRooney is following in the footsteps of his wife Coleen, who was runner-up on I'm A Celebrity in 2024."If you're going in you want to win it," he said. "Coleen's already tried and obviously she finished second in the show so I'm here to bring that title back to the Rooney household."Rooney admitted that jumping out of a helicopter is his biggest fear. "I've been booked to jump out of a plane three times before and never made it on the plane," he said."I don't like snakes or what is in the water either - I don't go in the sea."Image source, ITVImage caption, Ade Adepitan said he is "overwhelmed" to be the first wheelchair user on the showProducers are making adaptations to the Australian jungle camp so it is accessible for Adepitan.In a press statement, he said: "For me, this is a moment in time. Even if I go out in the first week, I will always be remembered as the person in a wheelchair. I am slightly overwhelmed. It's never been done before, and it never crossed my mind I would be the first."Keith Lemon comedian Leigh Francis is not among the official line-up but is rumoured to become a late addition.The last I'm A Celebrity series was the all-star version in South Africa, which was marked by heated arguments and walk-outs among the cast during the live final in April.

schema.headline: I'm A Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here! 2026 - see the line-up in full

title: Three Iran-backed suspects plotted attacks including RAF Fairford incident, US says
description: The US Department of Justice (DOJ) has announced charges against three Iran-backed operatives that it alleges were involved in a string of plots in th
body: The US Department of Justice (DOJ) has announced charges against three Iran-backed operatives that it alleges were involved in a string of plots in the US and Europe.The DOJ said Iranian agents most recently "orchestrated a terrorist plot at an air force base in the United Kingdom", saying they were involved in the major incident in September near RAF Fairford in the UK, where US armed forces were stationed.One man, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national, is accused of communicating with contacts in the UK from a prison in New York where he is awaiting trial on previous charges. The other two are accused of doing the same from Iran.Iran has strongly denied any involvement in the RAF Fairford incident.Seven men have been arrested in the UK over the incident, which came to light when suspicious vans were reported near the RAF base. Iranian Mohsen Mohajeri, Iraqi national Mohammad Ali al-Hassani and dual Iranian-Iraqi citizen Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi were charged in an indictment unsealed on Tuesday, the DOJ said.It accuses the trio of planning attacks in Europe that were carried out under the name of a purportedly new group with the pseudonym Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (The Islamic Movement of the People of the Right Hand - HAYI)."Of the 18 terrorist attacks in the spring of 2026 for which HAYI claimed responsibility in Europe, seven took place in the UK," the DOJ statement said. It added that the attacks involved "arsons, explosives, and in one instance, a near-fatal stabbing in London of two Jewish men, including a dual US-British citizen".Two Jewish men were stabbed in Golders Green, north London, in April. A suspect is due to stand trial next year."This eight-count indictment shows the determination of Iran to commit terrorist attacks in Europe and the US," FBI Director Kash Patel said.He added that one of the three "allegedly sent coded messages to assist in future acts of violence" from detention.Patel said the accused were involved in nearly 20 attempted attacks in support of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and the Iran-backed Iraqi militia Kataib Hezbollah.A major incident was declared on 27 September near the UK's RAF Fairford base, in the Cotswolds in Gloucestershire, after three suspicious vans were seen near the airbase.No explosive materials were found in the vans, but a quantity of petrol was seized.The DOJ said that in August, al-Hassani "allegedly directed and paid associates" in the UK to "conduct preparatory steps and arrange logistics for the RAF Fairford terrorist plot".On 22 August, al-Hassani paid one individual to "perform pre-operational surveillance of RAF Fairford's perimeter", the department said.In September, al-Hassani paid several people to help him prepare for the plot, the DOJ also alleged.According to its statement, this included "procuring vans and barrels of fuel, researching the purchase of chemical accelerants, including large quantities of potassium chloride, and purchasing metallic objects that could be used as explosive shrapnel".The suspects then gave the vans an appearance of being used by a fuel delivery business and a swimming pool supply business, the DOJ stated."On 26 September, al-Hassani allegedly tasked individuals to drive three vans, some of which were later determined to contain barrels of fuel, to the RAF Fairford base."The DOJ also said al-Hassani was "in frequent communication" with the van drivers and helped to direct them where to drive."At least two of the three vans, while en route to the perimeter of RAF Fairford, encountered a security roadblock and were not allowed to proceed on their intended route," it added.It was in the very early hours of 27 September, that the vans were spotted by a local farmer who was heading home from a party, and called the police.The Iranian embassy in London has said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" what it called "unfounded and malicious speculations" linking Iran to the incident.Two British nationals appeared in court last month in connection with the alleged Iran-linked plot.The US withdrew all its bombers from RAF Fairford after the incident, with President Donald Trump citing "some threats" to the base as the reason. RAF Fairford has been used by the US Air Force (USAF) for decades.In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from there to the Middle East for "defensive" strikes on Iran.In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".

schema.headline: Three Iran-backed suspects plotted attacks including RAF Fairford incident, US says

title: Why does Australia want Brits to swap Sydney for the outback?
description: In a Mexican restaurant in north-east Australia, the tacos are served by staff from France, Italy, Ireland and Argentina.Cairns has long attracted a y
body: In a Mexican restaurant in north-east Australia, the tacos are served by staff from France, Italy, Ireland and Argentina.Cairns has long attracted a young and transient international crowd, who enjoy the tropical lifestyle while earning money for travel.But one nationality is in shorter supply than it used to be."You get far fewer British backpackers looking for jobs here these days," says Mexicairns owner Peter McLeay.It's a trend McLeay has noticed since mid-2023, when a free trade deal between the UK and Australia kicked in.That agreement - as well as tariff-free trade in Tim Tams and Penguins - included special treatment for Brits on working holiday visas: exemption from having to find jobs in regional or remote places if they wanted to remain beyond a year.That, along with an increase in the age limit from 30 to 35 saw backpacker visas issued to Brits surging from 47,200 in 2023-24 to just over 77,000 in 2025-26, according to the latest Australian government data.Without the incentive to go regional, many are choosing to base themselves in the big cities, or, according to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, "Bondi or Coogee" - two of Sydney's most famous beachside suburbs.Now though, with Brits making up almost a quarter of all 323,000 backpacker visas issued last year, his government wants the free trade deal to be revisited."Many Brits don't treat it as a working holiday anymore. It's more a three-year career break," says Dan McConnell, general manager of the Mad Monkey backpacker hostel chain.He says Brits used to be the largest clientele at its Cairns accommodation but "now French outnumber British three to one"."We see the Brits get to Sydney, decide it's the coolest place in the world, and stay there," he adds.It's a privilege not enjoyed by working holidaymakers from other countries who must do at least 88 days of "specified regional work" in industries that need a seasonal or temporary workforce - including agriculture, fisheries, tourism and hospitality - if they want to qualify for a second year extension, and six months to stay a third year.Barely a month ago, Albanese ruled out forcing British backpackers to do the same, accepting it as part of the trade deal.But, under pressure from businesses here in Far North Queensland and other regional Australian communities, who are concerned about a lack of labour, the mood music has changed.Last week Albanese met UK counterpart Andy Burnham at the meeting of Commonwealth leaders in the Caribbean.And alongside AI, gender violence online and the AUKUS defence pact, backpackers were on the agenda.Despite speculation in the Australian media, no immediate announcement was made. Albanese instead told reporters that he had pushed for a change in the rules on backpackers and that Burnham had been "very constructive about it"."We'll work those issues through over coming weeks," he said adding that the free trade agreement was not set in stone and tweaks could be made "if there are good policy reasons".Backpackers make up one in seven farm jobs across Australia, with about 52,000 people on working holiday visas doing jobs in horticulture each year, according to the National Farmers Federation.It welcomed Albanese's discussions with Burnham, but said the issue of worker shortages in agriculture was far broader than the UK deal.Of greater concern are wider proposals, announced in September, to cut net migration into Australia, under political pressure from the resurgent right wing populist One Nation party and the opposition coalition.That includes an overhaul of the working holiday visa system, introducing a ballot for backpackers wanting to extend their stay – capped at 45,000 for people wanting a second year in Australia (down from 57,000 who qualified this year) and just 5,000 allowed to remain for a third year (compared with 31,000 this year).This, the federation says, is "a low blow".Those plans are still out for consultation, but immigration officials have slowed processing rates for some working holiday visa applications and paused them from several countries.Tourism Tropical North Queensland chief executive Mark Olsen has also been among those lobbying Albanese in Canberra - telling him that backpackers brought both the spending power and the temporary labour needed to fill seasonal roles in a region famed as a gateway to the Great Barrier Reef and the Unesco world heritage listed Daintree rainforest.Young Brits temporarily living and working in this region peaked at around 20,000 he says. Now it's closer to 11,000."Numbers have dropped significantly since the UK free trade agreement kicked in when border arrangements returned to normal [after the pandemic] in 2023 ," he said.Cairns restaurateur Fintan Rafferty says that of about 180 staff on his payroll across four venues, only five are British. Prior to the visa rule change, that was closer to 25.UK workers came with good skills in hospitality and "were willing to work, and to work flexible hours", he told the BBC.And, he said, it was a two-way street. "The pay is very good, the conditions are very good. And one of the great things about the 88-days rule is that it forces people to travel. It's enriching their experience."Bucking the trend, at the bar of Gilligan's backpackers, Paige Tomlinson serves vodka and soda with plenty of ice and a broad South Yorkshire accent.The 27-year-old, from Barnsley, has been in Cairns for four months, attracted by the "chilled" lifestyle and local waterfalls."Most people prefer Sydney and they question me all the time why I'm here," she laughs. "But I got to Sydney and I just didn't like it. It was too busy, too much like London and I don't like London."She says she'd like to see the regional work requirement brought in for all Brits,  "getting them out their comfort zone"."If every other country's got to do it, why should we not?"About 200km north, at  Red Valley Farm in Lakeland, general manger Peter Inderbitzen agrees.Workers mainly from Tonga, hired on a Pacific labour scheme, pick bananas there year-round.But Inderbitzen also relies heavily on backpackers, especially at peak avocado season, employing about 25 people for a couple of months each year."It's very short, sharp, get it done, get it out kind of work," he told the BBC. "But without those pickers, the avos stay on the tree."While a few British backpackers were still applying for work, numbers had "completely dropped off" since the rule change, said Inderbitzen, who'd "love" to see British travellers having an incentive to head to the regions."As much as it wasn't perfect, [that programme] was working."Back in Cairns, most of the young Brits the BBC tracks down are on tourist visas - but many want to return for a working holiday.Among them is Ethan Phillips, 23, from Buckinghamshire who has been having way too much fun to keep up to date with what politicians have been discussing."It makes sense for them to want us to do [regional work] again," he says. "I mean I'd rather not do it, but if we have to, it's only three months … it can't be that bad."

schema.headline: Why does Australia want Brits to swap Sydney for the outback?

title: In Mississippi, voters await cliffhanger Senate result with hope and frustration
description: Figure caption, Watch: BBC talks to Mississippi voters awaiting the Senate resultByBrandon DrenonMississippiMississippi's nailbiting wait to find out
body: Figure caption, Watch: BBC talks to Mississippi voters awaiting the Senate resultByBrandon DrenonMississippiMississippi's nailbiting wait to find out who won the southern state's Senate race is nearly over a week after the US midterm elections, in a contest that could deliver their first Democratic senator in nearly four decades.Scott Colom, the Democrat, holds a lead of about 2,500 ballots - less than 1% - over his Republican opponent, the incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith, according to the latest tally.If he wins, Colom would become the Magnolia State's first black senator in over 140 years.He would also pad the Democratic Senate majority-elect to 55 seats, with a knife-edge race in Alaska still to be called.The Democrat's razor-thin advantage has defied political gravity in a conservative fortress that President Donald Trump won in 2024 by over 22 points.State law holds that the deadline to certify results is this Friday, but thousands of postal and affidavit ballots remain uncounted.Affidavit ballots are ones that were not immediately accepted because of a discrepancy such as lacking proper ID on election day.In such cases, voters are asked to fill out a provisional ballot and return to resolve the issue. The deadline for both affidavit and mail-in ballots is on Tuesday.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Colom would be Mississippi's first black senator in over 140 yearsState officials estimate between 12,000 and 20,000 affidavit ballots were cast. As of Tuesday morning, roughly 15,500 had been processed – a difference that could be enough to swing the race.A Colom victory would wipe away a Republican winning streak in Mississippi that dates back to 1982.It would add to a string of Democratic successes nationally this election, including a landslide majority in the House of Representatives.Each party has sent teams of lawyers into Mississippi, setting up the possibility for legal challenges over the result.Image caption, Journey Moore said she hopes Colom can make historyAs the sun began to set on campus at Jackson State University, a historically black college in Mississippi, students walking through the tree-shaded lawns spoke to the BBC about the race.Many of them voted this year for the very first time. All of them said they had cast their ballot for Colom."I really feel like a change is what we need," 18-year-old Jamyria Dunn told the BBC."I've had some amazing days in my life," she continued, "but seeing Mississippi, this state in particular, turn blue, would really bring a light to my heart that people just would not understand."Dunn's friend, Journey Moore, told the BBC how excited she would feel if Colom won, leaving his mark on African-American history."On a scale of one to 10, it's definitely 1,000," she said."I'm witnessing it, and I'm a part of it. It's pretty great."Image caption, Trump voter Keith Moore said the president had not delivered in his second termThe BBC also visited Brookhaven, in Lincoln County, where Hyde-Smith was born and where Trump won a whopping 72% of votes two years ago.Party loyalty here was on stark display, with everyone saying either they didn't vote or they voted for Hyde-Smith.No-one denied the cost of living had gone up, but few here blamed Trump or Hyde-Smith."It always seems, no matter who's in office, there's a spike in gas prices. There's always a war. Things are always going up and down," said Travis Powe, a 29-year-old logger who voted for Hyde-Smith.Keith Scott, a Trump supporter, said both parties had been "attacking Trump at all angles, which was why we voted for him".Still, Scott said the race in Mississippi was unexpectedly close because the president had not delivered during his second term."Trump and his administration did not hold up what they ran on. Bottom line," Scott said."And the people like me that voted for him the first two times, that saw the benefits in his first term, we've seen none of it in his second."Image caption, Lifelong Republican Lee Barry said he wished Hyde-Smith had campaigned moreDown the street from the railroad tracks cutting through the centre of town was Lee Barry, also a lifelong Republican."The price on gas is really high, so that cuts into your pocket," Barry said. "And then you go into the grocery store, prices are high."You get your shopping cart, and you got five things in it, and it's 100 bucks before you get out of there."So, I think that hurt her a good bit," he said about Hyde-Smith, adding that he also thinks she "should have been out a little bit more" on the campaign trail.The race was never supposed to be this close.Colom appeared to be riding a national wave of resentment against Republicans, with the party suffering several defeats this election in typically conservative strongholds like Texas, Kansas and Iowa.Voter backlash against Trump's Republican party has been driven in large part by economic woes, blamed on his administration's tariffs and war with Iran, according to exit polls.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Trump flew into the state to campaign for Hyde-Smith last monthColom, a local prosecutor, used the national mood to his advantage, highlighting his opponent's support for Trump's tariffs and giving her the nickname "Cindy High Prices".The Democrat campaigned aggressively, visiting all of Mississippi's 82 counties.Hyde-Smith's campaign assailed Colom as a puppet of billionaire liberal donor George Soros, whose family has helped fund the Democrat's political campaigns.The Republican was criticised by her opponents for a lack of public appearances.Democrats accused her of insensitivity when she told voters worried about the price of beef that "you have so many proteins to choose from". The Colom team spun the remark into a viral attack ad.The race also became competitive because of Mississippi's large black population, who are expected to have turned out in record numbers this election.Early exit polls show the state's black voters, who historically vote Democrat, drifted even further to the left this year, giving Democrats 91% of their votes.

schema.headline: In Mississippi, voters await cliffhanger Senate result with hope and frustration

title: Christmas toy rush being driven by squishies and building sets
description: Traditional games, squishies and building sets are helping to drive a bumper year for toy sales, figures show.The data comes ahead of the crucial Chri
body: Traditional games, squishies and building sets are helping to drive a bumper year for toy sales, figures show.The data comes ahead of the crucial Christmas run-in for retailers, which peaks at 23 toys sold every second in the UK.The number of toys sold up to October was 17% higher than the same period last year and growth is at a 10-year high, according to research company Circana.The increase comes despite consumers' cost-of-living pressures, and there are signs that some of the biggest growth in sales is for toys priced between £5 and £10.Despite relatively low sales in recent years, the toy sector has been buoyed by sales to "kidults".The kidult market - which is toys and games for those aged over 12 - has been growing, particularly as adults buy toys for themselves.This growth has continued with a 22% increase in the value of sales in the first half of the year.But Melissa Symonds, UK toys director at Circana, said that toys for children - which still represents the majority of sales - had recorded a good year so far.Growing public debate around children's screen time and the role of technology meant squishy toys, stickers and building sets such as Lego were popular."Connected toys account for less than 1% of market sales, showing that traditional, hands-on play remains overwhelmingly popular," she said.

schema.headline: Christmas toy rush being driven by squishies and building sets

title: Jacob Bethell out of England's Australia tour and doubt for South Africa Tests
description: Jacob Bethell has been ruled out of England's white-ball tour of Australia and is a huge doubt for the Test tour of South Africa following the recurre
body: Jacob Bethell has been ruled out of England's white-ball tour of Australia and is a huge doubt for the Test tour of South Africa following the recurrence of a knee injury.Bethell has not played for England since July after suffering discomfort in his right knee while making 91 in a one-day international against India at Lord's.He had surgery in September and looked set to return down under when he travelled to Australia for the series that begins with the first of three one-day internationals in Perth on Friday.But the 23-year-old did not play in the warm-up match against Western Australia at the weekend and suffered what England have described as a "setback" in training earlier this week.Bethell underwent a scan and is now set to return home to see a specialist.England have called up Sussex all-rounder James Coles as cover, while uncapped seamer Eddie Jack has also been added to the one-day squad as a replacement for Josh Tongue, who had previously been ruled out with a toe injury.Following the three ODIs, England play five T20s in Australia, before the Test series in South Africa begins on 17 December.Bethell's continued absence is a huge concern for England, given the time he has already missed and his importance across all three formats.It is also a huge blow for Bethell, whose 154 in the final Test against Australia in January was one of the few highlights of England's dismal Ashes tour. Instead of being able to build on that innings, he has been stalled by the knee injury.The Warwickshire man was named in the squad for the three Tests in South Africa on Monday.At the time, selector Marcus North admitted England did not know who would make way from the team that beat Pakistan 3-0 during the home summer in order to accommodate Bethell's return.Opener Emilio Gay and Jordan Cox, batting at number three, both came into the England Test side for that series and one of them looked set to be left out of the final XI in South Africa.Now, both Gay and Cox could be set for further opportunities to stake their long-term Test credentials.In the summer, Ollie Pope was recalled to the Test squad as the spare batter in Bethell's absence.Pope is due to be with England Lions in South Africa in a tour that overlaps with the Test series, so the Surrey man looks a strong contender to be promoted if Bethell is ruled out.James Rew, who has one Test cap, and uncapped Durham opener Ben McKinney have both been in strong form on England Lions' white-ball tour of West Indies and would be other options to replace Bethell in South Africa.Speaking before the first one-day in Australia, Test captain Joe Root told BBC Sport: "It's disappointing for Jacob. I don't know much more. I know how hard he works and everything he's done to get himself right."Hopefully it's not too serious and he's not out for too long."

schema.headline: Jacob Bethell out of England's Australia tour and doubt for South Africa Tests

title: Tatjana Smith switches allegiance from South Africa to Netherlands
description: South Africa's most decorated Olympian Tatjana Smith was in tears as she announced that she has switched allegiance to the Netherlands.The 29-year-old
body: South Africa's most decorated Olympian Tatjana Smith was in tears as she announced that she has switched allegiance to the Netherlands.The 29-year-old won four Olympic breaststroke medals, including two golds, before retiring after the Paris 2024 Games.She came out of retirement in September and hopes to compete in the 50m breaststroke as the event makes its Olympic debut at the 2028 Games in Los Angeles.Smith, whose maiden name was Schoenmaker, wiped away tears as she read a letter addressed to South Africa, saying that "dreams can change as we grow".Smith has dual citizenship because her father is Dutch.She said she has "always been Dutch and South African" and that this is an opportunity to "explore another part of my identity and heritage that I've never experienced through sport".She said it also offers her "greater high-performance support and the potential to build a more sustainable career" because the "financial and practical challenges of swimming were among the reasons my previous career became difficult to sustain".Smith has previously said that financial worries, which included a dispute with Swimming South Africa over prize money, contributed to her decision to step away from the sport.Swimming South Africa has been approached for comment.Smith won four world and Commonwealth gold medals between 2018 and 2023.She won gold in the 200m breaststroke and 100m silver at the Tokyo Olympics in 2021, before adding 100m gold and 200m silver in 2024."Representing South Africa was a childhood dream come true, and it's a chapter I will always look back on with immense pride and gratitude," she said on social media., external"The people, the memories and everything we achieved together will always be part of me. But dreams can change as we grow."This next chapter is about embracing another part of who I am, falling in love with the journey and discovering what more I'm capable of."I'm excited for what lies ahead, and I truly hope you'll continue to be part of the journey with me."Smith, who said she will continue to live and train in South Africa, is set to represent the Netherlands for the first time at the short course World Championships from 1-6 December.She acknowledged that her switch "may disappoint or break the hearts" of some supporters.The Ministry of Sport, Arts and Culture in South Africa said it was aware of the "problems at Swimming South Africa"."The country was delighted to see her return to the pool, but South Africa does not own her," a statement read."Tatjana's choice belongs to her and it should not be turned into a political weapon."Gayton McKenzie, Minister of Sports, Arts and Culture, said: "Every medal, every record and every anthem she gave us belongs to our history forever. We now have to share her with the Netherlands."

schema.headline: Tatjana Smith switches allegiance from South Africa to Netherlands

title: Lindsey Vonn has ninth operation since Olympic crash
description: "I've been waiting all these nine months so my bones could heal and we could fix the ACL and my bones healed which is great news. "But obviously now I
body: "I've been waiting all these nine months so my bones could heal and we could fix the ACL and my bones healed which is great news. "But obviously now I have the ACL and that means another six to nine months."While racing in the Olympic downhill in Cortina - nine days after rupturing ligaments in her left knee - Vonn struck a gate and crashed 13 seconds into her run.The 2010 Olympic downhill champion previously revealed the operations had meant she did not have to have her leg amputated.Vonn, who is regarded as one of the greatest alpine skiers of all time, retired in 2019 after suffering numerous leg injuries.She made a shock return in 2024 after a partial right knee replacement.Vonn has won 84 World Cup races - second in the all-time women's list behind compatriot Mikaela Shiffrin.

schema.headline: Lindsey Vonn has ninth operation since Olympic crash

title: Why is Scotland's housing shortage getting worse?
description: ByPhil SimAndrew Picken and Aimee StantonBBC ScotlandUpdated 5 hours agoIt is three years since Scotland's largest cities declared "housing emergencie
body: ByPhil SimAndrew Picken and Aimee StantonBBC ScotlandUpdated 5 hours agoIt is three years since Scotland's largest cities declared "housing emergencies", followed months later by the nation as a whole.Since then, homelessness has hit record levels while the cost of renting or buying property has continued to rise.The solution to this crisis would appear straightforward - build more houses.But delivering this is more complicated, with responsibility falling to central and local government as well as to private housebuilders.Scottish ministers claim the country boasts the UK's highest rate of housebuilding , externalbut the pace is falling, and there are questions about whether the right homes are being built in the right places.So far, 13 Scottish councils have declared housing emergencies for a variety of reasons.They include rising pressure on homelessness services, high levels of people in temporary accommodation and a lack of affordable homes compared to lengthy waiting lists. Homelessness has increased to a record level, with Scottish government data showing, external more than 19,000 households in temporary accommodation paid for by councils - a 10% rise on the previous year.This includes 10,715 children living in temporary accommodation, such as a bedsit.A total of 35,000 households were assessed as being homeless or threatened with homelessness in 2025-26.As of March this year, there were more than 140,000 applications on council waiting lists for social housing.This figure does not include some large authorities like Glasgow which runs its social housing through housing associations, and has more than 6,000 live applications waiting.The overall social housing stock, external held by councils and housing associations has been rising since 2017 - the year after the Right to Buy scheme was abolished in Scotland - but has only recovered to its 2004 level.In March this year, there were 89,000 fewer social homes available than when the Scottish Parliament was reconvened in 1999 - despite a 9% rise in Scotland's population over the same period.While demand for social and affordable housing has been rising, the total number of homes actually being built has been falling.The housebuilding sector was only starting to recover from the 2008 financial crash when the Covid pandemic hit.In the 2025-26 financial year, a total of 17,640 new homes were completed according to Scottish government figures, external - the third year in a row where the figure had fallen.There is little prospect for an immediate improvement, as the number of new projects started over the last two years were the lowest since 2012-13.As to why this is happening, housebuilders point to a range of factors.The sector faces familiar problems with the cost of doing business, with construction materials particularly vulnerable to inflationary shocks like that which followed the war in Ukraine in 2022.Industry bodies also complain about a lack of suitable land, external earmarked for building, and say it takes too long for planning permission to be given to new developments.Red tape is also a concern. Homes For Scotland - which represents about 200 housebuilding firms - says the "regulatory burden being imposed by government" over recent years has added tens of thousands of pounds to the cost of a new-build home.They note that Chancellor John Healey promised in his UK budget not to make major changes to building regulations for the rest of the parliamentary term.Recent examples in Scotland include a levy to address unsafe cladding on tall buildings, new rules requiring "climate-friendly" heat sources and better energy efficiency.Scottish Housing Secretary Shirley-Anne Somerville told BBC Scotland News that ministers were alive to the concerns of housebuilders, but that these standards helped reduce energy bills and improved housing for disabled people.Are homes being built in the right places?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The rate of new build homes being completed has slowed in recent yearsThere is a notable disparity in rates of building in different parts of Scotland, with construction particularly concentrated in the area around Edinburgh.In 2025-26, 32% of the new homes completed in Scotland were in the Lothians.If you add in Fife, which is also a popular area for people commuting to the capital, then this corner of the country accounts for 39% of all new homes built, despite only having 23% of the population.Look to the west and the figures flip around; Glasgow and the surrounding councils have 32% of the population, but only 26% of the housebuilding.This is true even in relatively affluent areas with high rates of population growth, like East Renfrewshire - where just 87 new homes were completed last year.Glasgow has a homelessness problem so acute that the city council is spending almost £70m a year putting people up in hotel rooms.Along with Edinburgh, the city has been declared to be in a state of "systemic failure" by the Scottish Housing Regulator.Glasgow faces particular pressure with refugee households seeking support, with 44% of the 8,025 homelessness applications last year from people with refugee status or leave to remain - compared to 16% across Scotland as a whole.And yet there were fewer new home "starts" there last year than in East Lothian, a more rural area with one sixth the population, with city leaders in Glasgow blaming rising construction costs.Plans have just been announced for 6,500 new affordable homes to be built on brownfield sites - previously developed land which is currently unused - over the next six years.The council also says it has identified 59 sites across the city as potential locations for another 12,173 new homes, which could be built by 2032 if funding becomes available. It is also looking at repurposing disused shops for housing.Image source, GettyImage caption, Flats like these ones in Edinburgh  were built as council homes but now are a mix of social and private housingThere has been a historic shift in Scotland's population towards Edinburgh, with the capital's financial and service sector booming while areas in the west struggle to recover from the decline of traditional industries.Demand for homes around the capital has driven up property prices. Edinburgh, Midlothian and East Lothian all feature in the top four areas in Scotland, external with the highest house prices, all well above the national average, external.This makes it attractive to housebuilders seeking a return on investment - and it also means businesses in the construction trade and related supply chains are more likely to thrive there.Meanwhile those in the industry say there are fewer small-to-medium sized building firms in more rural areas to take projects forward.Higher prices in the east of Scotland have meant problems with affordability for some.A study for Shelter Scotland, external suggested that 62% of newly-formed households - people entering the housing market for the first time, such as those leaving the parental home - in this area were unable to afford the current market. For Scotland as a whole, the figure was 55%.Are Scotland's house building targets being met? That same study suggested an extra 15,693 affordable homes need to be built each year to end the housing emergency.The Scottish government does not have an overall housebuilding target, but it did set one in 2022 for affordable homes - to complete 110,000 of them by 2032, external, with at least 70% available for social rent and 10% in island and rural communities.The latest figures show 36,500 completions towards this target.The Scottish Parliament Information Centre says that with just over five years left to go, this means on average 15,000 homes need to be delivered each year, external.In 2025-26, there were 6,832 completions as part of the Affordable Housing Supply Programme - down from a peak of 10,466 in 2022-23.So the rate of delivery needs to more than double, and then be sustained at record levels, if the target is to be met.Scotcast: Our housing shortage and the 'big city doughnuts'Martin Geissler is joined by Aimee Stanton and Phil Sim to crunch the numbers on how we’re getting on with housebuilding and discuss the current housing picture across the country.Ministers say they are committing £4.1bn over the next four years to support the delivery of "around 36,000 affordable homes".Builders have welcomed the longer-term certainty offered by this funding, but that would still only get half way to the 110,000 target with two years remaining.Modelling by the Fraser of Allander Institute, external think tank suggests it is more likely to take until late 2036.The Scottish government says it "remains focused" on achieving the 110,000 target, while acknowledging that it is "challenging".Somerville said it could be met through longer-term investment in publicly funded affordable housing schemes - through vehicles like the Scottish National Investment Bank - as well as support for private developers.The government is also setting up a new national agency next year - More Homes Scotland - which hopes to "remove barriers and accelerate housing delivery".

schema.headline: Why is Scotland's housing shortage getting worse?

title: Usman Khawaja: Former player refuses to name ball-tampering players in sandpaper scandal
description: The publisher of Usman Khawaja's autobiography has denied his promotional tour has been cancelled but says there have been "adjustments" to the schedu
body: The publisher of Usman Khawaja's autobiography has denied his promotional tour has been cancelled but says there have been "adjustments" to the schedule.Reports in the Australian media, external said the former Australia batter had pulled out of several engagements following an interview with broadcaster ABC in which he refused to name which national team players knew of ball tampering in the 2018 Test series with South Africa.Khawaja insisted in the interview that he wanted his former team-mates to take collective responsibility as a team, but did not want to be responsible for a "witch hunt" regarding specific players."The book tour is 100% still going ahead, we've just had to make some adjustments this week, but no major cancellation of the tour at all," said Khawaja's publisher Penguin in a statement to ABC.The fall-out from the series led to bans for captain Steve Smith, vice-captain David Warner and fellow batter Cameron Bancroft, but a Cricket Australia investigation found the national side's bowling attack were unaware of the ball-tampering.Australia's attack in the contentious third Test - Pat Cummins, Josh Hazlewood, Nathan Lyon and Mitchell Starc - remain fixtures in the national side.The quartet issued a joint statement in 2021 saying they "did not know a foreign substance was taken on to the field".Khawaja told ABC that he was simply "sharing my version of the truth" and "not calling for anything"."It's never been for me about pointing fingers and saying, 'he did this, he said that'. That's why even when I first wrote my edit there were names, there were lots of things, and I pulled it back. "Sometimes I'm very specific on things and sometimes they're a bit vague on things, and I do it on purpose because I'm trying to tell a story."My main objective here is always to try and take accountability as a team, to say, yes, this was happening. And even though one person did it or the captain knew about it and Davey Warner always took the heat for it, that it wasn't just them, that we were all involved in it as a team."Former team-mate Warner has said the claims in Khawaja's book are "100% accurate" and that "lies will eventually get out".Asked about Warner's comments, Khawaja said: "I'm not going to speak on behalf of Davey. I've tried my best to tell my story in an open and safe environment. "Twenty-two pages is what sandpaper is and I've tried my best in that to explain my version of events."I'm not here to inflame the situation any more. I was here to tell my truth, what I saw, what I felt and to stick with those three guys that were made out to be the only people who have taken it, and I wanted that to be shown."Pressed as to whether Cummins, who has been Australia's Test captain since 2021, knew of the ball-tampering, Khawaja said: "I'm not going to answer that.""This has never been a witch hunt for me. It's only been those three guys who've had to cop this flak for a long time," Khawaja added."I'm hoping other people will come up and talk about it honestly. That's what I'm hoping, but I'm not forcing anyone to do anything."You've got to remember Pat Cummins is a good friend of mine, Mitchell Starc, a lot of these guys, Shaun Marsh, Mitch Marsh, they're all very good friends of mine. All I've ever wanted is for us to take accountability as a team. I don't think that's a lot to say."Meanwhile, England batter Joe Root said "I don't want to speculate" when asked about the scandal in the build-up to his side's first one-day international against Australia on Friday.Questioned about the idea that ball-tampering was rife across the international game at the time, Root said: "I can only speak from my own experiences. That's not how I feel, no."

schema.headline: Usman Khawaja: Former player refuses to name ball-tampering players in sandpaper scandal

title: Mauricio Pochettino ready to accept Man Utd offer to replace Michael Carrick.
description: Mauricio Pochettino is ready to accept an offer from Manchester United to become their next head coach.United have opened talks with the Argentine abo
body: Mauricio Pochettino is ready to accept an offer from Manchester United to become their next head coach.United have opened talks with the Argentine about him potentially replacing Michael Carrick, who is expected to be relieved of his duties in the next 48 hours.Once Carrick's future is clarified, sources have told BBC Sport that USA manager Pochettino wants to take the job.The former Tottenham and Chelsea boss wants to remain respectful to the US Soccer Federation and will wait for United to make an official approach.The Red Devils would be required to pay $10m (£7.5m) to release Pochettino from his contract, which he only signed in August.The USA have a two-legged Concacaf Nations League quarter-final against Haiti over the next week. That means the timing of developments at Old Trafford could make things awkward, particularly if Pochettino, 54, was to leave midway through the current camp.But he views the prospect of managing United as a serious opportunity, with the expectation being he would accept the job were it formally offered.United have spoken to the ex-Argentina defender about their managerial position on three previous occasions - when Jose Mourinho was sacked in 2018, then in 2022 before the club appointed Erik ten Hag and again when the Dutchman was sacked in 2024.Carrick's future at United will be decided at a meeting in Monaco on Wednesday that will be attended by chief executive Omar Berrada, director of football Jason Wilcox and co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe.Berrada and Wilcox have flown to Monaco for one of their regular, planned meetings to discuss strategy around the football club.On this occasion, the main issue to be decided is Carrick's future and what should happen next.It is expected that Berrada and Wilcox's recommendation is for the head coach to go.Carrick, 45, was pictured arriving at the club's Carrington training base on Wednesday.United are 18th in the Premier League - inside the relegation zone - after winning just one of their first 10 games and none since August.It is the club's lowest position at this stage of a top-flight season since 1986-87, when they were 20th.Pochettino's first job in the Premier League was at Southampton from January 2013, before a five-year stint at Tottenham from 2014 that included a Champions League final appearance.He managed Paris St-Germain from January 2021 to July 2022 before spending the 2023-24 season in charge of Chelsea.Pochettino moved into international football by taking the USA job in September 2024, and led the co-hosts to the last 16 of the 2026 World Cup.While it may seem a touch immoral for Manchester United to be talking to a potential new manager before they have decided if their current one is staying or not, this kind of situation is not uncommon in football.Jose Mourinho had agreed a contract with United in 2016 before Louis van Gaal was sacked, which is how stories - including from BBC Sport - came out that the Dutchman would be dismissed as he was celebrating the FA Cup final triumph over Crystal Palace.Going further back, Mark Hughes was replaced immediately by Roberto Mancini at Manchester City in 2009. Hughes' imminent dismissal was reported on the morning of his final game in charge. It is impossible to reach that situation without talks taking place beforehand, and it would be naive to think they do not go on in a world in which agents are pushing clients for jobs that either do, or do not, exist or clubs are trying to gauge interest before making a decision.I have been told by one source the Pochettino terms to join United are more or less agreed. I have also been told if they decide to push on, United can decide whether the former Spurs and Chelsea boss remains with the USA team for their matches against Haiti.If he did stay, it would mean a sharp turnaround from a Tuesday night match - which finishes in the early hours of Wednesday - to be at Carrington for preparations before United's game against Liverpool at Anfield on 22 November.There are a lot of gaps to fill in yet, not least whether Carrick will be dismissed or not.But it seems more likely there will be clarity on that on Wednesday, and from that the rest of the jigsaw pieces should start to slot into place.

schema.headline: Mauricio Pochettino ready to accept Man Utd offer to replace Michael Carrick.

title: England: Does Jordan Pickford finally face serious competition from James Trafford?
description: When England head coach Thomas Tuchel decided to pick Leeds United goalkeeper James Trafford to face World Cup holders Spain at Wembley in the last in
body: When England head coach Thomas Tuchel decided to pick Leeds United goalkeeper James Trafford to face World Cup holders Spain at Wembley in the last international break, it sparked the first stirrings about preparations for life without long-time first choice Jordan Pickford.Tuchel made it clear Pickford was still England's number one pick, but the simple fact he decided to alternate keepers - playing Trafford in the 3-2 loss to Spain then victory against Czech Republic, before Everton's 32-year-old returned for the Wembley win against the Czechs and the 7-0 rout in Croatia - created intrigue and debate.England meet Croatia at Wembley on Thursday before facing the biggest test of their Uefa Nations League campaign when they play Spain in Madrid on Sunday.Tuchel maintains strong faith in Pickford, an outstanding performer for England, but Trafford has at least had the chance to stake his claim.Tuchel has suggested he may use a rotation system for the pair once more in the upcoming internationals, which will only increase scrutiny on England's goalkeeping position.Pickford's record is outstanding since he made his debut in a 0-0 draw against Germany at Wembley in 2017.In his time as first choice, England have once more emerged as major players on global stage, reaching the World Cup semi-finals in 2018 and 2026, as well as successive Euros finals at the delayed 2020 tournament and Euro 2024.Measured by Opta stats, Pickford has made only two errors leading to goals in 93 appearances, with 46 clean sheets and a 74% save ratio.Trafford's international career is in its infancy and, while former England goalkeeper Paul Robinson says Pickford remains Tuchel's undisputed first choice, he believes the head coach's recent strategy is a sensible one.Robinson told BBC Sport: "It obviously remains to be seen what Thomas Tuchel does in these two England games, but I could see exactly what he was doing by giving James Trafford game time in the last round of matches."We are so guilty as a nation of taking one goalkeeper to a tournament who has 70, 80, 90 caps, then the two of three below him could have less than double figures combined."Robinson's point is proved by the statistic that 80 of Pickford's appearances have been competitive games, with 33 at major tournaments, made up of 19 at the World Cup and 14 at European Championships."Competitive and tournament caps give you the type of experience you can't get as a number two or three keeper," said Robinson."James Trafford is only 24 and has four caps - two of them competitive - so you can see exactly what Tuchel is doing, looking ahead to a situation where England's recognised number one is not available to him, or there is a drop off in form."We saw the last selections and all thought Jordan Pickford's place is under threat and James Trafford is going to be the next number one. I don't think Thomas Tuchel saw it as starkly or simply as that."It's a conversation that will definitely take place down the road, but not now. Jordan is England's first choice, in my opinion, rightfully so given his consistency and performances over such a long period."This is a debate and conversation for the future definitely because Father Time catches up with everyone eventually and the manager needs to have a contingency plan, but Jordan Pickford very much remains number one and Thomas Tuchel has said as much."I don't think Jordan Pickford is under threat for his jersey on a permanent basis  any time soon, irrespective of the next selection, but what Tuchel is doing reinforces the impression that he has to be at the top of his game and maintain high standards, which he certainly has been doing when I've watched him this season."The biggest compliment I can pay Jordan Pickford is that when you have got that England goalkeeper's shirt, everybody thinks somebody else should be doing it. I know that from personal experience."You're there to be shot at, but there has been no noise around Jordan Pickford for a very long time now."It has worked both ways for Jordan, James and Thomas Tuchel, and worked very well. Jordan knows he can't rest on his laurels and he will just play regardless. He has to be playing well."Is James Trafford challenging Jordan Pickford right now? Yes he is - if Jordan Pickford isn't playing very well and Jordan Pickford is making errors."None of the above are true right now because he's playing well for Everton and has done nothing wrong for England."Robinson also drew on club form to support Pickford's case. Since the start of the 2024-25 season, only Arsenal's title-winning keeper David Raya has more clean sheets in the league than Pickford at Everton.Raya has 39 clean sheets in that time, while Pickford has 27, with Robinson saying: "That's a superb record and all logic tells you Pickford will have to work a lot harder for his clean sheets than David Raya."Trafford staked his claim in those Nations League games against Spain and the Czech Republic, putting him at the forefront of Tuchel's thoughts as the main understudy to Pickford.Crystal Palace's Dean Henderson is now back in contention after injury and hoping to add to his six caps, although he has not been included in Tuchel's latest squad.Trafford moved to Leeds United from Manchester City in the summer in a British record deal for a goalkeeper that could be worth up to £45m.It came after a £23m move to City from Burnley the previous summer, when his hopes of becoming Pep Guardiola's first choice were unexpectedly ended by the decision to sign Gianluigi Donnarumma from Paris St-Germain.Robinson said: "James Trafford needed that move to Leeds United and Leeds United needed a keeper of his level. This is a match made in heaven."And don't forget, in a Premier League career with Burnley, Manchester City and Leeds United, Trafford has only played 42 Premier League games – just a little more than a full season – and one Champions League game. He needs this experience."He's got a huge amount of potential, with his quality, all-round goalkeeping and mental approach. He has the potential be England's future number one, which Tuchel clearly sees him to be."He has the mentality to reach the very top, which is very difficult because not all goalkeepers have that. It's a tough place to be, a very lonely place to be, but he has the ability to cope with that situation."I was at Bournemouth when he made an error in the Leeds United defeat there, but, knowing the type of character he, is it won't faze him. It won't bother him. Because of his personality and his character traits, he has got the ability to go right to the top."You'd think Dean Henderson will be back in the squad in due course once he has played more games."Jason Steele is in there again, but he's a mentor figure behind the scenes, not someone who will ever start or threaten the established goalkeepers."If you rewind back 18 or 24 months, you had Nick Pope, Sam Johnstone, James Trafford, Dean Henderson, Aaron Ramsdale and Jordan Pickford - a real plethora of England goalkeepers."Now Nick Pope is not playing at Newcastle United, Sam Johnstone's not in the equation and Aaron Ramsdale is nowhere near."Ramsdale's decline has been dramatic after leaving Arsenal for Southampton in August 2024, with a loan spell at Newcastle United proving to be unsuccessful. He has effectively been fourth choice at Saints this season, failing to make matchday squads.Robinson said: "I find Aaron Ramsdale's situation very sad because I believe he's a goalkeeper able to play at the top level."He should be in this conversation because he's a goalkeeper I really like, but he's been very unfortunate with selection of clubs and the way their season have gone. I still think there is time for him to come back into the reckoning."For now, though, if there is a conversation to be had about England's goalkeepers, then Jordan Pickford and James Trafford is that conversation, with Jordan still very much the number one right now as far as I'm concerned."

schema.headline: England: Does Jordan Pickford finally face serious competition from James Trafford?

body: Depending on the contract you have, data charges may apply for accessing the internet on your mobile device.If you are not sure about the potential charges, please ask your mobile network provider.
